title: Ada Lovelace: The First Programmer
summary: How Ada Lovelace, a math-loving girl from London, wrote step-by-step instructions for Charles Babbage's machine and became known as the first computer programmer.
poll: Imagination is just as important as math for inventing new technology.

versions.title: Ada and the Math Machine
versions.text:
Ada Lovelace was born in 1815. She lived in London. Her mom loved math. So Ada had lots of math lessons.

Ada was sick a lot as a child. She had to stay in bed. But her mind was busy. She drew plans to fly. She got the plan from birds.

At 17, she met a man. His name was Charles Babbage. He liked to invent things. He had a plan for a big machine. It could do sums. Ada was glad. She wished to learn all of it.

Then he made a plan for a new machine. It was not built. But Ada wrote a lot on it. She wrote out steps for it. The steps told it how to find some hard numbers. A list of steps for a machine is a program. So lots of folks say Ada wrote the first one.

Ada had a big dream, too. She said a machine might make songs one day.

Ada died young. Now kids all over the world learn to code. One code is named for her.

Ada Lovelace was born in London in 1815. Her mom loved math. She made sure Ada had lots of math lessons.

Ada was sick a lot as a child. She had to stay in bed for a long time. But her mind kept busy. She even drew plans to fly. She got the plans from birds.

When Ada was 17, she met a man named Charles Babbage. He liked to invent things. He had a plan for a big machine. It could do sums. Ada was thrilled. She wanted to learn all about it.

Then Babbage made a plan for a new, better machine. It was never built. But Ada wrote a lot of notes on it. She wrote out the steps the machine would need. The steps would help it find a set of hard numbers. A list of steps for a machine is called a program. That is why many people call Ada the first person to write one.

Ada had a big dream, too. She said that one day a machine might make music.

Ada died young. Today, kids all over the world learn to code. A code is even named Ada for her.

versions.title: Ada Lovelace: The First Programmer
versions.text:
Ada Lovelace was born in London in 1815. Her mother loved math. She made sure Ada had math and science lessons from a young age.

As a child, Ada was often sick. She had to stay in bed for months. But her mind kept working. When she was about twelve, she even drew plans for a flying machine, after she watched how birds fly.

When Ada was 17, she met a man named Charles Babbage. He liked to invent things. He had built part of a machine that could do sums. Ada was thrilled, and the two became friends.

Next, Babbage planned a new and much better machine. It was never built. But Ada wrote long notes about it. In her notes, she wrote out the steps the machine would follow to work out a set of hard numbers. A list of steps for a machine is called a program. That is why many people call Ada the first person to write a program.

Ada also had a big dream. She said that one day a machine might do more than math. It might even make music.

Ada died young, at 36. Today, kids all over the world learn to write programs. A computer language is even named Ada in her honor.

Ada also had a big idea. She said that one day a machine might do more than math. It might even make music.

Ada died young, at the age of 36. Today, students around the world, including many in Saudi Arabia, learn to write programs. A computer language is even named Ada in her honor.

Ada could also imagine what others could not. She said that one day such a machine might do more than math. It might even make music.

Ada died young, at the age of 36. Today, students around the world, including many in Saudi Arabia, learn to write programs. A computer language is even named Ada in her honor.

versions.title: Ada Lovelace: The First Programmer
versions.text:
Ada Lovelace was born in London in 1815. Her father was the famous poet Lord Byron, although Ada never really knew him. Her mother was passionate about mathematics, so she ensured that Ada studied mathematics and science from an early age, even though very few girls received such a rigorous education during that period.

As a child, Ada was frequently ill and had to remain in bed for months at a time, yet her imagination never stopped working, and when she was approximately twelve, she systematically studied how birds fly and produced detailed plans for a flying machine of her own.

When Ada was 17, she met an inventor named Charles Babbage, who had constructed part of a machine that could calculate, or perform arithmetic automatically. Ada was so fascinated by it that she wanted to understand every component, and the two soon became close friends who exchanged numerous letters about mathematics and machinery.

Later, Babbage designed a considerably more powerful machine called the Analytical Engine, which was intended to follow instructions stored on punched cards, although it was never completed during his lifetime. An Italian engineer wrote an article about the engine in French, and Ada was asked to translate it into English; she did, but she also contributed her own extensive notes, which ended up approximately three times longer than the original article when they were published in 1843.

In one note, Ada wrote out precise instructions, step by step, demonstrating exactly how the engine could calculate a complicated series of numbers. Today, a careful sequence of steps like this is called an algorithm, and when it is written for a machine, it becomes a program, which is why many historians consider Ada the first computer programmer.

Ada was also a visionary who could imagine possibilities that others could not, and she suggested that one day such a machine might accomplish much more than arithmetic, and that it might even compose music, an idea that seemed extraordinary to her contemporaries.

Ada died young, at the age of 36, and although the Analytical Engine was never constructed, her ideas proved remarkably accurate once electronic computers appeared roughly a century later. Today, students around the world, including many in Saudi Arabia, learn to write programs, and a computer programming language is named Ada in her honor.

versions.title: Ada Lovelace: The First Programmer
versions.text:
Ada Lovelace entered the world in London during 1815. Her father was the renowned poet Lord Byron, although Ada scarcely knew him throughout her childhood. Her mother, however, possessed a genuine passion for mathematics, and this ensured that Ada received hard instruction in mathematics and science from an unusually early age. Few girls received such demanding educational opportunities during that particular historical period.

As a child, Ada suffered frequent, debilitating illnesses that confined her to bed for months at a stretch, yet her fertile imagination never ceased its restless operation; when she reached approximately twelve years of age, she studied avian flight patterns and subsequently produced detailed engineering plans for a flying machine fully of her own original design.

When Ada reached the age of seventeen, she encountered an inventor named Charles Babbage, who had already constructed a functional portion of a bold machine capable of calculating, or automatically performing arithmetic operations. Ada found herself so fully fascinated by this device that she resolved to comprehend every individual component. The two soon developed a close, lasting friendship characterized by extensive correspondence concerning mathematics and mechanical engineering.

Later, Babbage designed a more bold and powerful machine designated the Analytical Engine. This was intended to execute instructions stored upon punched cards. However, it unfortunately remained uncompleted throughout his entire lifetime. An Italian engineer composed an article describing this engine in French, and Ada was later commissioned to translate it into English; she dutifully completed this task, but also contributed her own extensive explanatory notes, which ultimately proved approximately three times lengthier than the original article when they were officially published in 1843.

Within one particular note, Ada carefully articulated precise, sequential instructions demonstrating exactly how the engine could calculate a particularly complicated mathematical series. Today, such a carefully ordered sequence of procedural steps is officially designated an algorithm. When such an algorithm is written for execution by a machine, it correspondingly becomes a program, which explains why many historians consider Ada to be the very first computer programmer in recorded history.

Ada also functioned as a genuine visionary, possessing the remarkable capacity to imagine future possibilities that eluded the comprehension of her peers, and she boldly suggested that such a machine might eventually accomplish more than mere arithmetic calculation, potentially even composing original music, a suggestion that struck her peers as fully great and implausible at the time.

Ada died tragically young, at merely thirty-six years of age. Although the Analytical Engine itself was never ultimately constructed during either of their lifetimes, her prescient ideas proved astonishingly accurate once functional electronic computers finally emerged roughly a century later. Today, students throughout the world, including large numbers across Saudi Arabia, routinely learn to write computer programs. A particular computer programming language bears the name Ada, honoring her basic and lasting contributions to the field.

versions.title: Ada Lovelace: The First Programmer
versions.text:
Ada Lovelace entered the world in London during the year 1815. Her father was the internationally renowned poet Lord Byron, although Ada scarcely knew him personally throughout her formative childhood years. Her mother, however, possessed a genuine and abiding passion for mathematics, and consequently ensured, with considerable deliberation, that Ada received rigorous instruction in mathematics and the natural sciences from an unusually early age, notwithstanding the inconvenient fact that remarkably few girls received such demanding educational opportunities during that particular restrictive historical period.

As a child, Ada suffered frequent, genuinely debilitating illnesses that confined her to bed for months at a continuous stretch, yet her remarkably fertile and irrepressible imagination never once ceased its restless intellectual operation; when she reached approximately twelve years of age, she systematically and methodically studied avian flight patterns in considerable detail and subsequently produced remarkably detailed engineering plans for a flying machine entirely of her own original conception and design.

When Ada reached the age of seventeen, she first encountered an inventor named Charles Babbage, who had already successfully constructed a functional portion of an ambitious mechanical device capable of calculating, or automatically performing complex arithmetic operations without human intervention. Ada found herself so thoroughly and immediately fascinated by this remarkable device that she resolved firmly to comprehend every individual mechanical component, and the two soon developed a close, enduring intellectual friendship characterized by extensive, substantive correspondence concerning mathematics and mechanical engineering.

Subsequently, Babbage designed a considerably more ambitious and mechanically powerful machine designated the Analytical Engine, which was specifically engineered to execute programmable instructions stored upon punched cards, although it unfortunately remained permanently uncompleted throughout the entirety of his lifetime. An Italian engineer composed a detailed article describing this engine in French, and Ada was subsequently commissioned to translate it faithfully into English; she dutifully completed this translation task, but additionally contributed her own extensive explanatory notes and annotations, which ultimately proved approximately three times lengthier than the original source article when they were formally published in 1843.

Within one particularly significant note, Ada meticulously and systematically articulated precise, sequential instructions demonstrating exactly how the engine could successfully calculate a particularly complicated mathematical series of numbers. Today, such a carefully ordered sequence of procedural steps is formally designated an algorithm, and when such an algorithm is specifically written for subsequent execution by a mechanical or electronic machine, it correspondingly becomes what we now call a program, which explains precisely why numerous historians and computer scientists consider Ada to be the very first computer programmer in all of recorded history.

Ada additionally functioned as a genuine intellectual visionary, possessing the remarkable and rare capacity to imagine future technological possibilities that entirely eluded the comprehension of her own contemporaries, and she boldly and prophetically suggested that such a machine might eventually accomplish considerably more than mere arithmetic calculation, potentially even composing original musical compositions, a suggestion that struck her contemporaries as thoroughly extraordinary and almost fantastically implausible at the time it was proposed.

Ada died tragically young, at merely thirty-six years of age, and although the Analytical Engine itself was never ultimately constructed during either of their respective lifetimes, her remarkably prescient theoretical ideas proved astonishingly accurate once fully functional electronic computers finally emerged roughly a century subsequently. Today, students throughout the entire world, including substantial and growing numbers across Saudi Arabia, routinely learn to write computer programs, and a particular, widely used computer programming language officially bears the name Ada, honoring in perpetuity her foundational and enduring contributions to the discipline of computer science.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to build a flying machine at home
How Ada Lovelace wrote steps for a machine and became known as the first programmer
Why kids should stay in bed when they are sick
How to write music on a computer
questions.why: The article tells about Ada's life and how she wrote the first program for Babbage's machine.

wrong.A: Ada drew plans to fly, but that is only one detail.
wrong.C: Being sick is part of her story, not the main idea.
wrong.D: Ada only dreamed that machines might make music one day.

questions.stem: Who made sure Ada had lots of math lessons?
options: Her teacher at school
Charles Babbage
Her mom, who loved math
Her best friend down the street
questions.why: The article says Ada's mom loved math and made sure Ada had math lessons.

wrong.A: The article does not talk about a school teacher.
wrong.B: Ada met Babbage when she was 17, after her lessons began.
wrong.D: No friend is named in the article.

questions.stem: What did Ada write in her notes about the new machine?
options: A story about birds
The steps the machine would need to find hard numbers
A long letter to the king and the queen of her country
A plan for a new house
questions.why: The article says Ada wrote out the steps the machine would follow to find a set of hard numbers.

wrong.A: Ada studied birds to plan flying, but that was not in her notes on the machine.
wrong.C: There is no letter to a king in the article.
wrong.D: The article says nothing about a house.

questions.stem: In the article, what is a program?
options: A list of steps for a machine
A big, heavy book full of math problems
A type of flying machine
A song made by a computer
questions.why: The article says a list of steps for a machine is called a program.

wrong.B: A program is a list of steps, not a book.
wrong.C: Ada's flying plans were not a program.
wrong.D: Music was only Ada's dream for the future.

questions.stem: Why do many people call Ada the first person to write a program?
options: Because she built the very first computer in the whole world
Because she was the first person to study math
Because she invented the flying machine
Because she wrote out the steps a machine would follow
questions.why: Ada wrote the list of steps for Babbage's machine, and a list of steps for a machine is a program.

wrong.A: The machine was never built, and Babbage planned it.
wrong.B: Many people studied math before Ada.
wrong.C: Ada only drew plans for flying.

questions.stem: Ada had to stay in bed as a child, but she drew plans to fly. What does this tell you about her?
options: She did not like to learn
She was curious and kept thinking even when she was sick
She wanted to be a doctor
She was afraid of the many birds she saw outside her window

wrong.C: The article does not say she wanted to be a doctor.
wrong.D: She studied birds to learn how to fly; she was not afraid.

questions.stem: Ada said a machine might make music one day. What can you infer?
options: She hated music
She already owned a machine at home that could play music
She could picture machines doing more than math
She thought machines were useless
questions.why: Saying a machine might make music shows she imagined machines doing jobs beyond sums.

wrong.A: Nothing in the article says she hated music.
wrong.B: Machines like that did not exist in her time.
wrong.D: She was excited about machines, not against them.

questions.stem: How is the article mostly organized?
options: As a list of computer parts
As a list of steps for how to make a program
As a problem and a solution
In time order, from Ada's birth to today
questions.why: The article starts with her birth in 1815, moves through her life, and ends with kids learning to code today.

wrong.A: The article is about a person, not computer parts.
wrong.B: It tells about Ada; it does not teach how to make a program.

MID.prompt: Explain how Ada Lovelace's work went beyond simply translating an article. Use details from the text.
checklist: I explained what Ada was asked to do.
I explained what she added and why it mattered.
I used at least two key words from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: Ada was only asked to translate an article about Babbage's engine from French into English, but she went far beyond that task. She added her own notes, which ended up about three times longer than the original article, and in one note she wrote out clear, step-by-step instructions showing how the engine could calculate a special set of numbers. Because that list of instructions is a program, many people consider her notes, not just her translation, to be her true achievement.

HIGH.prompt: Ada Lovelace's ideas came long before modern computers existed. Explain why her work still matters today, using the words algorithm and visionary.
checklist: I explained what Ada wrote and why it counts as a program.
I used algorithm and visionary correctly.
I connected her ideas to computers today.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Ada Lovelace's work still matters today because, in her notes, she wrote out a step-by-step algorithm showing how Babbage's engine could calculate a set of numbers, which is why many people call her the first computer programmer even though the machine itself was never built. She was also a visionary, since she imagined that such a machine might one day do far more than math, even compose music, an idea that sounded impossible in her time but describes exactly what modern computers can do. Her early algorithm and her visionary thinking about what machines could become connect directly to the programs that run on every computer today.
